sections.title: About this edition
text: This journal records my four-day school observation at Amity International School, Mayur Vihar, from 1 to 4 December. It brings together daily notes, photographs, reflections and what I learned as a B.Ed. student.

This readable edition was prepared from my 49-page handwritten journal. The wording has been edited for clarity, related notes have been grouped, and photographs have been cropped from the supplied pages. The year is not recorded in the source. These are my observations during the visit; the journal is a student record, not a school-issued certificate.

sections.title: Acknowledgements
text: I thank Dr. Alka Mudgal, HOD; Dr. Seema Agnihotri, school internship teacher; and Dr. Jaya Mukherjee, faculty coordinator, for their support. I also thank Ms. Meenu Kanwar, Principal of Amity International School, Mayur Vihar, and Ms. Anshu Bhatnagar, school coordinator, for arranging the observation and guiding us through the school routines.
I am grateful to the teachers and students who allowed us to learn from their daily work and took time to speak with us.

sections.title: Why I observed
text: School observation helped me connect ideas from teacher education with classroom practice. I wanted to understand how teachers plan and explain lessons, use teaching-learning materials, manage a class and respond to students with different needs.

I also wanted to see the work that supports teaching: timetables, assemblies, learning spaces, staff coordination and activities outside lessons. Watching these routines gave me a clearer idea of the responsibilities I would take on as a teacher.

sections.title: The school as recorded in my notes
text: My original notes describe Amity International School, Mayur Vihar, as a co-educational, English-medium day school offering Classes I-XII and following the CBSE curriculum. They record its establishment in 1999, its place in the Ritnand Balved Education Foundation school group, and CBSE affiliation number 2730586.

During the visit I observed classrooms, science and computer labs, libraries, sports spaces, art and sculpture rooms, an auditorium and the Atal Tinkering Lab. The school setting let me study both subject teaching and the organisation of daily school life.

sections.title: My areas of attention
bullets: How teachers explain ideas, ask questions and check understanding.
How classroom routines and respectful communication support attention.
How students take part in practical work, reading and school activities.
How teachers, coordinators and staff work together.

sections.title: Morning routines
text: I reached the school at about 8:10 a.m. with my peers and faculty coordinator Dr. Jaya Mukherjee. Morning prayers took place in classrooms, while late arrivals assembled on the ground. I began by watching how students moved into the school day and how the morning routine was managed.
Ms. Anshu Bhatnagar assigned us to teachers. This gave each of us a place to observe and helped us understand what to look for during the visit.

sections.title: Social Studies in Classes IX-D and VIII-B
text: With Ms. Nitika, I observed Social Studies lessons in Classes IX-D and VIII-B. She explained the content while keeping track of attention and discipline. Students had opportunities to respond, and her interaction with them helped maintain the flow of the lesson.

I paid attention to the balance between explanation and student participation. Classroom management happened throughout the teaching, through instructions, questions and attention to students, rather than being a separate task at the end.

pages.title: Lessons, laboratories and preparation

sections.title: Science labs
text: I visited the physics and chemistry labs. I noticed ventilation, laboratory attendants and safety arrangements. Students carried out experiments while teachers explained the steps. Watching this made me think about the preparation and supervision needed for practical work.

sections.title: A senior classroom
text: I also observed a Class XII lesson with Ms. Priya on democracy, the legislature and the judiciary. The lesson relied more heavily on the teacher's explanation, and I noticed less student participation than in the earlier classes. This difference became an area for reflection in my journal.

sections.title: Preparing for school activities
text: Later, I joined peers in preparing craft and game ideas for the school carnival planned for 20 December. At the end of the day, we met Ms. Anshu Bhatnagar and discussed our assignments. She asked us to arrive by 7:50 a.m. the next morning.

Our peer discussion brought together observations from different parts of the school, including primary activities, noticeboards and robotics preparations. Listening to others helped me compare my own classroom observations with their experiences.

pages.callout: I began to notice how explanation, student participation and classroom routines work together.

sections.title: Beginning the day
text: I reached school at about 8 a.m. Late arrivals assembled for the anthem before going to their classes. After a briefing with the coordinator, I observed Ms. Sushmita's periods from 8:20 to 9:00 a.m. and from 11:30 a.m. to 12:05 p.m.

sections.title: Class X-C
text: The Class X-C lesson focused on organising examination answers. Ms. Sushmita explained the paper pattern, discussed common mistakes and clarified students' questions about writing answers according to the examination requirements. I saw how this support could help students understand what a question asks and how to present a response.

sections.title: Class XII: Kinship, Caste and Class
text: In a Class XII lesson on Kinship, Caste and Class, the teacher used examples from the Mahabharata, including Draupadi and the Pandavas and Arjuna and Subhadra. These cultural references were used to explain kinship and marriage practices, including polyandry and polygamy.
The lesson was mainly lecture-based. I found that familiar stories made the explanation easier to follow and helped connect the topic with examples students could recognise.

pages.title: Reading, practical work and student initiative

sections.title: Preparing an awareness programme
text: I helped students with craft work for the PCOS/PCOD awareness programme scheduled for 3 December. They took responsibility for their materials and preparation. I appreciated seeing students contribute to an activity through their own ideas and work.

sections.title: Junior and senior libraries
text: I visited the junior library, used up to Class VIII, and the senior library for Classes IX-XII. I was told that the junior library had about 15,000 books and the senior library about 8,000. Books were organised by subject, and students could borrow them for reading at home.
I liked the practice of asking students to write book reports when returning books. It connected borrowing with a response to what they had read.

sections.title: Biology observation
text: In the biology lab, students learned about plant cells with a smartboard presentation using video and audio, followed by microscope work. I saw the explanation and practical observation used in sequence.
At about 1:45 p.m., we met to share our observations and discuss the next day's work.

pages.title: Making, presenting and caring for students

sections.title: Carnival preparation
text: I arrived at about 7:50 a.m. and was assigned to work with Mr. Singhal. In the physics lab, I worked with peers on a Roll the Dice game board for the 20 December carnival. We prepared three number tracks running from 1 to 11.

sections.title: The awareness programme
text: I watched students present their PCOS/PCOD awareness materials. They explained their posters confidently and spoke with ease about the topics they had prepared. Their presentation made me think about how responsibility for a task can encourage student participation.

sections.title: Medical room and playground
text: I visited the ground-floor medical room and observed the nurse's role in checking students, arranging rest and contacting parents when needed. This helped me see another part of the care that supports the school day.

On the playground, senior students played football and younger students took part in supervised activities such as standing long jump and bar holds. The activities reminded me of my own school days. I noticed students' enjoyment, the teacher's supervision and practical arrangements such as a rack for jackets.

sections.title: Computer learning
text: In the computer lab, a projected demonstration was followed by students working at individual computers. The rows allowed the teacher to watch their work and move between students who needed help. I noticed how the room layout supported supervision.

sections.title: Chess and table tennis
text: Students were absorbed in chess. In the table-tennis room, three tables were used for supervised practice. These spaces gave students opportunities to practise concentration, skill and cooperation outside subject lessons.

sections.title: Art, craft and sculpture
text: In the art and craft room, students worked individually and in groups. Materials were issued using a teacher's slip, which helped organise their use. The sculpture room contained raw, dried and painted clay work, including animal figures, decorative pots and small models.

At our end-of-day discussion, peers described activity-based learning in primary classes and classroom greetings. Comparing these observations helped me understand how teaching changes with the age of the learners.

sections.title: Listening to students
text: I reached school at about 8 a.m. and attended the coordinator's briefing. Ms. Sushmita had no scheduled classes that day, so I observed her counselling Class XII students. She listened to their concerns and career aspirations and offered guidance.
This showed me how a teacher supports students through conversation and attention to their needs, alongside subject teaching.

sections.title: Assembly in the auditorium
text: I attended an assembly for Classes IX-XII in the basement auditorium, organised by Class IX-A. Different classes took turns organising assemblies. Students played the keyboard, spoke about responsible use of social media and performed classical and hip-hop dance.

Their peers encouraged the performers. Mr. Singhal added humour and encouragement, which helped make the gathering welcoming. I saw how a student-led assembly gives learners practice in organising, speaking and performing in front of others.

pages.title: Display work and the Atal Tinkering Lab

sections.title: Working on noticeboards
text: With peers, I worked on three third-floor noticeboards and a staffroom board under Ms. Neetu's guidance. We cleaned and repaired damaged areas and put protective film on the three boards. For the staffroom board, we used a white chart-paper background with gold and black borders.
This was a practical example of the preparation and maintenance that teachers carry out around lessons and school activities.

sections.title: Robotics preparations
text: I visited the Atal Tinkering Lab on the ground floor near the medical room. Students were working with model racing cars, drones and robots as part of preparations for a robotics competition.

They asked questions and worked intently on their projects. I noticed that this type of work also challenges teachers to respond to complex questions. It helped me understand the value of curiosity and problem-solving in a learning space.

pages.title: The spaces and routines behind teaching

sections.title: Walking through the school
text: My tour covered the basement, ground floor and four upper floors. I noted the public announcement system, CCTV, fire-safety equipment, drinking water and washrooms. The arrangement of rooms and facilities helped me think about how a school plans for students' movement, learning and care.

sections.title: Floor-by-floor notes
bullets: Ground floor: principal's office, pantry, medical room, Atal Tinkering Lab and classrooms.
First floor: library, chess room, Montessori and Maths lab, and classrooms.
Second floor: physics, chemistry and biology labs, and classrooms.
Third floor: sports room, Cambridge English class and classrooms.
Fourth floor: art room, sculpture room and classrooms.

sections.title: Closing the visit
text: In the library, I watched primary learners take part in a number game. They were excited by the activity and enjoyed learning through play.

At the end of the visit, the pre-service teachers met Ms. Anshu Bhatnagar and the vice-principal. We thanked the coordinator and principal, listened to their advice and brought the four-day observation to a close.

pages.title: What I noticed about learning

sections.title: Classroom communication
text: Across the four days, I observed clear explanations, real-life and cultural examples, and teachers who responded patiently to students' questions. Respectful communication helped teachers maintain discipline. These observations gave me examples of classroom practice to connect with my B.Ed. learning.

sections.title: Participation varied with the lesson
text: Students were generally attentive and responsive in the classes I observed. In senior classes, participation varied. I noticed fewer responses during long explanations and more interest when teachers used examples or invited discussion.

The awareness programme, carnival preparations, robotics work and library games gave me further examples of students taking an active part in learning. I need to consider how a task allows students to contribute, alongside the content I want to explain.

sections.title: Materials and technology
text: Projection equipment, computer labs and the Atal Tinkering Lab were part of the school's learning environment. In biology, a presentation was followed by microscope work. In the computer room, a demonstration was followed by individual practice. I saw how the sequence of explanation and activity shaped students' work.
The libraries also mattered. Organised books, borrowing and book reports gave students a routine for reading and responding to what they read.

pages.callout: I want to plan lessons that give students time to ask, explain, discuss and try things for themselves.

pages.title: Teaching depends on more than a lesson

sections.title: Facilities and care
text: The school had science and computer labs, libraries, sports areas, art and sculpture rooms, an auditorium and a medical room. I also noticed drinking water, washrooms and safety arrangements. These were part of the everyday conditions in which teachers and students worked.
School buses were available, while some students travelled independently. The visit helped me see how transport, care and the organisation of spaces affect the school day.

sections.title: Co-curricular activities
text: The student-led assembly was organised with clear roles. Students' awareness posters showed preparation and a willingness to explain their work. Art and sculpture displays let me see what students had made, while sports activities combined participation with teacher supervision.
These activities gave students opportunities to practise teamwork, responsibility, creativity and confidence. They also required teachers to plan, supervise and coordinate.

sections.title: Coordination and school culture
text: Meetings with Ms. Anshu Bhatnagar helped us understand daily assignments and routines. Sharing observations with peers showed me how the different parts of the school fitted together. The counselling session gave me a view of the care teachers provide through listening and guidance.
I experienced the school environment as respectful and organised during the visit. That is my reflection on the four days I observed.

pages.title: The teacher I am learning to become

sections.title: Understanding a real lesson
text: I learned to watch how a teacher begins and structures a lesson, chooses examples, gives instructions and responds to doubts. Stories and cultural references can help make an explanation accessible. I also saw that the amount of student participation changes with the way a lesson is taught.
For my own practice, I want to make space for questions and discussion and check whether students are following an explanation.

sections.title: Classroom management
text: Seating arrangements, movement around the room, eye contact, routines and timely feedback all affected classroom management. Teachers used their presence, tone and instructions to guide students.
I need to learn how to respond to students who lose attention or hesitate to ask a question. Fairness and a supportive classroom environment matter to the way I want to teach.

sections.title: Student behaviour and learning
text: Students showed interest in activities that were practical, engaging and relatable. They enjoyed collaborative work. Senior students participated more when examples and discussion were included than during a pure lecture.

This observation encouraged me to pay closer attention to the relationship between the task, the students' responses and the teacher's next step. A respectful, friendly teacher-student relationship is also part of the classroom I want to build.

sections.title: Learning through activities
text: Arts, sports, robotics, craft and awareness work gave students different ways to participate. Student-managed assemblies let them take responsibility and work with others. These experiences helped me think about how learning can continue outside a subject period.

sections.title: Resources and organisation
text: I learned how organised learning spaces support students' work. Libraries encouraged reading and skill-based activities; projectors, computers and the Atal Tinkering Lab supported other kinds of learning. I also became more aware of safety, cleanliness and medical support.

The visit helped me understand school timetables, assemblies, counselling and daily planning. Teachers maintain records, coordinate activities and prepare yearly, monthly, weekly and lesson plans. Clear communication among teachers and staff helps these routines work.

sections.title: Responsibilities beyond teaching
text: A teacher also counsels and mentors students, supports projects and competitions, watches classroom behaviour and helps maintain an inclusive environment. Observing these responsibilities helped me understand the emotional, academic and social support involved in the role.

sections.title: Connecting with teacher education
text: In my original reflection, I connected the labs, robotics, art and student-led assembly with ideas I had studied in relation to NEP 2020: experiential learning, creativity, critical thinking, technology use and learning beyond academic content. These are connections I made as a student during the observation.

sections.title: My next steps
text: I want to be patient, prepared, respectful and able to engage students. I need to plan lessons carefully, adapt them to students' needs and handle classroom challenges calmly. Reflecting on each day can help me recognise what worked and what I need to improve.

sections.title: What I take from these four days
text: My four-day observation at Amity International School, Mayur Vihar, helped me understand school routines and the responsibilities of a teacher. I could connect ideas from the B.Ed. programme with explanations, activities, classroom management and student support that I saw during the visit.

I learned that teaching requires subject knowledge, communication, classroom management, empathy and the ability to adapt. The experience strengthened my wish to become a reflective, responsible and creative teacher. I want to use these observations when I plan and teach my own lessons.

sections.title: Source and editorial record
text: Prepared from the supplied file 1000035936.pdf: 49 scanned pages containing 26 numbered handwritten content pages and accompanying photographs. This edition preserves the four-day sequence, the main observations and the first-person reflections. Repeated statements have been combined and spelling and grammar have been edited.

The dates 1-4 December follow the original journal. No year has been added. Approximate times and reported library counts remain approximate. School details are retained as recorded in the notes. Photograph captions identify the subjects shown in the source; they do not add new evidence.
Source references in the footer use the PDF's scan-page numbers, not the handwritten page numbers. The original scan is retained separately and is not the file published in the portfolio.
